A beginner can compare the pitch of different thicknesses and areas, and note that the size of the resonating cavity affects the volume. In Africa instruments are sometimes set in river valleys and similar places so that the sound carries further; in Vanuatu most islands lay them flat on the ground, while the central islands stand them upright and carve them.

裂縫鑼屬體鳴樂器，琴身通常以木或竹製成，多取一段樹幹鑿空成共鳴腔，再於表面切出裂: The slit gong is an idiophone. Its body is usually made of wood or bamboo, most often a section of trunk hollowed out into a resonating cavity, with one or more slits cut in the surface; the sounding body is the tongue formed by cutting the wood or bamboo itself, and different areas or thicknesses give different pitches. It is played by striking the edge of the slit with a stick or mallet, and the source does not state the material of the sticks. Apart from wood, bamboo and the sticks, the materials of the other parts are not recorded.
裂縫鑼的音色具有獨特的穿透力，帶有明亮而乾脆的質感，卻又不失木質的溫潤厚度。其音: The slit gong has a distinctive carrying power, with a bright, dry quality that does not lose the warm thickness of wood. Its range varies with material and size, usually spanning the middle-low to the treble, from a dull, thick low hum to a sharp high note. When struck, the sound reverberates and resonates inside the hollow wooden or bamboo cavity and decays naturally. Compared with a traditional drum the slit gong lacks the depth of resonance a drumhead gives, but its timbre seems rawer and purer; compared with metal percussion its sound is softer and friendlier, with a strong folk character. Its resonance lasts well, which gives the sound clear musical definition.
裂縫鑼起源於非洲和太平洋島嶼地區，是人類最古老的打擊樂器之一。早期的非洲部落利用: The slit gong originated in Africa and the Pacific islands and is one of the oldest percussion instruments of humanity. Early African communities made slit gongs from hollowed wood and used them to send signals, in sacrificial rites and at social gatherings. Peoples of Melanesia and Polynesia in the Pacific also developed similar instruments independently, and they became an important part of tribal culture. With the exploration and trade of the colonial period the slit gong's influence gradually spread to Asia and the Americas. In Asia, parts of Southeast Asia such as Indonesia and the Philippines brought it into local musical traditions. After the twentieth century ethnomusicologists began to study the instrument systematically, and it gained academic recognition. Today the slit gong survives not only in traditional tribal cultures but has also been taken up by modern musicians, and it is a valued part of the world's musical heritage.

The slit gong, also called the slit drum, is an idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 111.243. It has no drumhead: a hollow resonating cavity is made of bamboo or wood, and one or more slits are cut in its surface; some designs are cut on three sides and leave one side to form a tongue. The player strikes the edge of the slit or the tongue with a drumstick or mallet, and the whole instrument vibrates; tongues of different thickness or area can produce different pitches. It is distributed across Africa, Southeast Asia and Oceania; in Africa it is often set in river valleys and similar places for long-distance communication, in Vanuatu and elsewhere there are horizontal or upright carved wooden drums, and the wooden drums of the Wa people are associated with sacrificial rites and festival performance.
